John 1.summary: John opens by identifying the eternal Word as both with God and divine, the agent of creation and source of life; the Word becomes flesh, revealing God's glory through Jesus Christ (John 1:1–18). John the Baptist denies that he is the Messiah and bears witness to Jesus as the Lamb of God (John 1:19–34). Two of John's disciples follow Jesus; Andrew brings Simon, and Jesus calls Philip, who invites Nathanael (John 1:35–51). The chapter announces Jesus' identity and begins showing how testimony leads others to him.
John 1.whereWeAre: The opening connects Israel's scriptural traditions with a Judean baptism setting and movement toward Galilee; its precise calendar year is unspecified. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 1 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. Interpretations that extend beyond the text should be marked as interpretations.

John 2.summary: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus' mother tells him that the wine has run out. Jesus directs servants to fill stone jars with water, which he turns into wine; John calls this the first of his signs, through which he manifests his glory and his disciples believe (John 2:1–11). Jesus subsequently travels briefly to Capernaum (John 2:12). In Jerusalem at Passover he drives vendors and money changers from the temple precincts, protests making his Father's house a marketplace, and speaks of raising the temple of his body in three days (John 2:13–22). Though many see his signs, Jesus does not entrust himself to them because he knows human hearts (John 2:23–25).
John 2.whereWeAre: The narrative places the temple incident at a Passover pilgrimage in Jerusalem; its chronological relationship to Synoptic Gospel presentations is debated. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 2 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. John 3.summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and Jewish leader, visits Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that one must be born from above or again, of water and Spirit, to enter God's kingdom; their exchange introduces the Son of Man being lifted up and God's love in giving the Son (John 3:1–21). Later, John the Baptist explains that his own ministry must diminish while Jesus' grows. He rejoices as the bridegroom's friend and stresses the significance of responding to the Son (John 3:22–36). The chapter joins new birth, divine love, faith, and humble witness.
John 3.whereWeAre: The dialogue takes place within first-century Jewish conversations about purification, Israel's teacherly traditions, and the hope of God's kingdom. John 4.summary: Leaving Judea for Galilee, Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well near Sychar. He offers living water, reveals knowledge of her life, and explains worship in spirit and truth; she tells her town, and many Samaritans believe (John 4:1–42). Jesus then returns to Galilee, where a royal official asks him to heal his dying son. The official trusts Jesus' word and later learns the child recovered at the hour Jesus spoke; John calls this another sign (John 4:43–54). Both accounts show faith developing across social boundaries and at a distance.
John 4.whereWeAre: The account crosses the cultural and religious divide between Jews and Samaritans in the region between Judea and Galilee. John 5.summary: At a Jewish festival in Jerusalem, Jesus heals a man disabled for thirty-eight years at the pool of Bethesda, telling him to take up his mat and walk (John 5:1–9). The healing on a Sabbath provokes dispute with Judean religious authorities, and Jesus responds by describing his work as inseparable from the Father's, including giving life and exercising judgment (John 5:10–30). He appeals to the testimony of John, his works, the Father, and the Scriptures, and challenges people who search the Scriptures yet refuse to come to him for life (John 5:31–47).
John 5.whereWeAre: The chapter is set at Jerusalem's pool complex during an unnamed festival; identification of the festival and some site details remain uncertain. The precise identity of the unnamed festival and variant spellings of Bethesda/Bethzatha are disputed. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 5 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. John 6.summary: Jesus feeds a large crowd with five loaves and two fish near the Sea of Galilee; the people interpret the sign as prophet-like, while Jesus withdraws when they seek to make him king (John 6:1–15). He walks on the lake toward his disciples at night (John 6:16–21). In Capernaum he challenges the crowd to seek enduring food and calls himself the bread of life, connecting belief with the Father's gift and future resurrection (John 6:22–59). Many disciples find the teaching difficult and leave, while Peter speaks for the Twelve in confessing that Jesus has words of eternal life (John 6:60–71).
John 6.whereWeAre: The setting includes Galilean lakeshore villages and Passover approaching, explaining both pilgrimage associations and manna imagery. John 7.summary: Jesus' brothers urge him to go to the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem, but he initially remains in Galilee and later goes privately (John 7:1–13). He teaches in the temple, leading to disputes about his learning, Sabbath healing, his origin, and whether he is the Messiah (John 7:14–36). On the festival's final great day, he invites the thirsty to come to him for living water; the narrator explains this as referring to the Spirit (John 7:37–39). The crowd divides, officers hesitate to arrest him, and Nicodemus asks whether the Law permits judging someone without hearing him (John 7:40–52). Some Bibles include 7:53 as the start of a disputed later textual passage.
John 7.whereWeAre: The scene is Jerusalem during Sukkot, the autumn Feast of Tabernacles; precise ritual details varied across periods, so specific reconstructions should be qualified. John 7:53 introduces the textually disputed account that continues at 8:11. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. John 8.summary: In the KJV, the chapter opens with the account of a woman accused of adultery and Jesus' challenge to her accusers; this passage (John 7:53–8:11) is absent from many early manuscripts and is widely regarded as a later addition to John's text (John 8:1–11). Jesus then calls himself the light of the world and debates his testimony, his relationship to the Father, and the consequences of unbelief (John 8:12–30). He teaches that abiding in his word brings freedom through truth, disputes appeals to descent from Abraham, and speaks of the devil as father of lies (John 8:31–47). The argument culminates in his claim, 'Before Abraham was, I am,' after which opponents take up stones (John 8:48–59).
John 8.whereWeAre: The debate is placed in Jerusalem's temple precincts in a first-century Jewish context; the disputed opening cannot simply be treated as securely original to John. The passage about the accused woman (7:53–8:11) is missing from the earliest major Greek witnesses and is widely understood by textual scholars as secondary to John; the KJV includes it. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 8 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. Interpretations that extend beyond the text should be marked as interpretations.

John 9.summary: Jesus encounters a man blind from birth. Rejecting a simple blame of the man's condition on personal or parental sin, he makes mud, sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, and the man returns seeing (John 9:1–12). Because the healing occurred on a Sabbath, Pharisees question the man, his parents, and Jesus' authority (John 9:13–34). The formerly blind man becomes more forthright about Jesus and is expelled from the group interrogating him. Jesus seeks him out, receives his faith, and speaks of judgment in which those claiming to see may remain blind (John 9:35–41).
John 9.whereWeAre: The action occurs in Jerusalem and refers to the pool of Siloam, a known feature of the city's water system; the full procedure and social repercussions come from John's account. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. John 10.summary: Jesus compares himself to the gate of the sheep and the good shepherd, contrasting his care with thieves and hired workers. He says he lays down his life for the sheep and will gather other sheep into one flock (John 10:1–21). At the winter Festival of Dedication in Jerusalem, opponents press him to say plainly whether he is the Messiah. Jesus points to his works, speaks of his sheep hearing his voice, and states that he and the Father are one (John 10:22–30). After renewed accusations of blasphemy he quotes Scripture in defense and withdraws across the Jordan, where many believe (John 10:31–42).
John 10.whereWeAre: The Dedication festival recalls the temple's rededication in the second century BCE; shepherding was familiar in Judean rural life and biblical royal imagery. John 11.summary: Mary and Martha send for Jesus because their brother Lazarus is ill, but Jesus arrives after Lazarus has been in the tomb four days (John 11:1–17). He speaks with Martha about resurrection and declares himself the resurrection and the life; Mary and other mourners weep, and Jesus is deeply moved (John 11:18–37). At the tomb he orders the stone removed, prays, and calls Lazarus out alive (John 11:38–44). Some witnesses believe, while others report to the authorities. The chief priests and Pharisees convene a council; Caiaphas argues that one man's death is preferable to national catastrophe, and a plot to kill Jesus develops (John 11:45–57).
John 11.whereWeAre: Bethany lies near Jerusalem; the narrative's political concern reflects the vulnerability of Judean leadership under Roman imperial rule. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 11 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. John 12.summary: Six days before Passover, Mary anoints Jesus' feet at a meal in Bethany, while Judas objects to the cost; Jesus relates the act to his burial (John 12:1–8). Crowds come to see Jesus and Lazarus, and the chief priests consider killing Lazarus too (John 12:9–11). Jesus enters Jerusalem riding a young donkey, fulfilling the narrative's interpretation of Scripture (John 12:12–19). Greek-speaking worshipers ask to see Jesus, who speaks of a grain of wheat dying to bear fruit, his approaching 'hour,' and being lifted up to draw people (John 12:20–36). John reflects on widespread unbelief despite signs, then summarizes Jesus' mission as light and saving truth (John 12:37–50).
John 12.whereWeAre: The action is near Jerusalem at Passover season amid crowded pilgrimage and heightened Roman sensitivity to royal claims. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. John 13.summary: Before the Passover, Jesus washes his disciples' feet during a meal, despite Peter's objections, and presents his humble service as an example for them (John 13:1–20). He announces that one of his own will betray him, gives bread to Judas, and Judas goes out into the night (John 13:21–30). Jesus then speaks of his coming glorification and gives a new commandment to love one another as he has loved them, saying this love will mark them as his disciples (John 13:31–35). Peter promises to follow him, but Jesus predicts Peter will deny him three times (John 13:36–38).
John 13.whereWeAre: A Jerusalem meal near Passover provides the setting, although precise chronology relative to Synoptic accounts is debated. John 14.summary: In a farewell discourse, Jesus encourages troubled disciples with the promise of his Father's house and says he is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:1–7). Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus explains that knowing and seeing him reveals the Father; he associates his works and the disciples' future prayer with the Father's purpose (John 14:8–14). Love for Jesus is expressed through keeping his commands, and he promises another Advocate, the Holy Spirit, who will teach and remind the disciples (John 14:15–26). Jesus gives them his peace and prepares them for his departure (John 14:27–31).
John 14.whereWeAre: This is a literary farewell discourse before Jesus' arrest, with echoes of Jewish testament and teacher-disciple farewell conventions. John 15.summary: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his Father the gardener, describing his disciples as branches that bear fruit by remaining in him (John 15:1–8). He calls them to remain in his love, keep his commandments, and love one another, treating them as friends rather than mere servants because he has shared the Father's purpose with them (John 15:9–17). He then warns that the world will hate his followers as it hated him, and says the Advocate, the Spirit of truth, will testify about him, as will the disciples (John 15:18–27).

John 16.summary: Jesus tells his disciples that exclusion and persecution lie ahead, warning that opponents may believe they are serving God (John 16:1–4). He explains that his departure will lead to the Advocate's coming, who will expose the world's error and guide the disciples into truth (John 16:5–15). Jesus describes a little while of grief that will turn to joy, comparing their future sorrow to childbirth (John 16:16–24). The disciples express confidence, but he warns they will scatter, even as he declares that he has overcome the world and offers peace amid trouble (John 16:25–33).
John 16.whereWeAre: The speech anticipates conflict between Jesus' followers and other communities; the exact social setting of John's audience remains debated. John 17.summary: Jesus prays to the Father, asking to be glorified so that he may give eternal life to those entrusted to him, and describing eternal life as knowing the Father and Jesus Christ (John 17:1–5). He prays for the disciples he has taught, asking that they be kept, made holy in the truth, and sent into the world as he was sent (John 17:6–19). He also prays for later believers who will trust through the disciples' message, that they may be one and thus bear witness to the world (John 17:20–26).
John 17.whereWeAre: The prayer belongs to the farewell narrative and reflects Jewish patterns of intercessory prayer and consecration language. John 18.summary: Jesus crosses the Kidron Valley to a garden, where Judas arrives with soldiers and officers to arrest him; Jesus identifies himself, and Peter cuts off the high priest's servant's ear before Jesus restrains him (John 18:1–11). Jesus is questioned by Annas; Peter denies knowing him three times near a charcoal fire (John 18:12–27). Jesus is brought before the Roman governor Pilate, who questions him about kingship and truth. Jesus says his kingdom is not from this world; Pilate declares he finds no case against him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas to be released instead (John 18:28–40).

John 19.summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged and mocked as king; despite declaring no guilt, he authorizes crucifixion under pressure (John 19:1–16). Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two others, with an inscription identifying him as King of the Jews. Soldiers divide his garments, and Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple (John 19:17–27). After saying he thirsts, Jesus declares 'It is finished' and dies; a soldier pierces his side, which John connects with Scripture (John 19:28–37). Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus wrap and bury his body in a nearby new tomb before the Sabbath (John 19:38–42).
John 19.whereWeAre: Roman crucifixion was a public punishment; the account is set in Jerusalem under Pilate during Passover preparations, with chronology debated across Gospels. Outside evidence establishes Roman crucifixion and Pilate's prefecture, not each specific detail of this crucifixion account. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 19 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. Interpretations that extend beyond the text should be marked as interpretations.

John 20.summary: Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it is dark and finds the stone moved; Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved run to see the empty tomb and burial cloths (John 20:1–10). Mary remains weeping, then encounters Jesus, initially mistaking him for the gardener, and reports seeing the risen Lord (John 20:11–18). That evening Jesus appears among the disciples, says 'Peace,' commissions them, and breathes on them with words about receiving the Holy Spirit (John 20:19–23). Thomas, absent from the first appearance, says he needs to see the wounds; eight days later Jesus appears again, and Thomas confesses him as Lord and God (John 20:24–29). John states his purpose: these signs are written so readers may believe and have life in Jesus' name (John 20:30–31).
John 20.whereWeAre: The narrative is situated in Jerusalem shortly after the crucifixion; the appearances are Gospel testimony rather than independently documented occurrences. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 20 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. Interpretations that extend beyond the text should be marked as interpretations.

John 21.summary: By the Sea of Tiberias, seven disciples fish at night without success. At dawn Jesus calls from shore and instructs them where to cast the net; they bring in a large catch of 153 fish and share bread and fish with him (John 21:1–14). Jesus asks Simon Peter three times whether he loves him and commands him to feed and tend his sheep, then speaks of the manner of Peter's future death (John 21:15–19). Asked about the beloved disciple, Jesus tells Peter to follow him rather than speculate about the other's fate; the chapter corrects a rumor that the beloved disciple would not die (John 21:20–23). A closing testimony identifies the beloved disciple as witness and notes that Jesus did much more than was written (John 21:24–25).
John 21.whereWeAre: The scene is at the Galilean Sea of Tiberias and uses fishing imagery; its placement as an epilogue and relationship to chapter 20 is discussed by scholars. The chapter reports specific sayings, conversations, and signs as part of John's narrative; not every narrated detail is independently corroborated. This background helps explain the setting of John 21 without equating a theological claim, a literary image, and an independently documented event. Interpretations that extend beyond the text should be marked as interpretations.
